catalog_quote: There is a length distinction in the vowels and between single and double (or geminate) consonants that is phonemic and important for proper pronunciation. The Sikaiana people speak of such contrasts as ‘heavy’ versus ‘light’, or ‘slow’ versus ‘rapid’. In the text, these distinctions are represented by doubling the consonant or the vowel. ... The following minimal pairs demonstrate the length distinction for vowels: aha ‘shell tool for making a net’ ahaa ‘cyclone’ aaha ‘open up’ ... taku ‘my’ takuu ‘axe’ These distinctions not only reflect vowel length, but also affect the stress patterns, since primary stress normally falls on the penultimate (second to last) vowel and secondary stress on every other preceding vowel (this corresponds with syllables). sources.quote: No statement on stress or accent anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent/stress: zero hits). Phonology gives the segment inventory, s/h variation, and notes that the native texts' double vowels 'in the present grammar ... has been abandoned' (p.165). Source material is a 1932 mission prayer book compiled by Guadalcanal missionaries, not fieldwork.
